When the evidence is ambiguous, programs often advance anyway and stop once human data confirms what earlier results suggested. AI that evaluates preclinical results as a whole, and compares them with outcomes for similar compounds, can flag weak candidates sooner.

metadata.author: Alex Philippidis

content.value:
Drug development still runs on long odds. Only 6.7% of drugs entering Phase I reach approval, an all-time low according to Citeline’s analysis of 2014-2023 programs. Timelines are stretching as well. A July 2026 study in JAMA Health Forum found that the median time from first human trials to reimbursement for new U.S. drugs grew over the past decade, with longer clinical development driving most of the increase.

AI is usually discussed as a way to speed up individual tasks like screening compounds, summarizing literature or drafting documents. The bigger payoff comes from using AI to connect discovery, lab work, data science and clinical operations, so lessons carry from one phase to the next.

Earlier, better-informed decisions

Target identification depends on synthesizing a huge, uneven body of evidence: published studies, genomic databases, patient registries, real-world clinical data and a company’s own experiments. AI can analyze these sources together and rank targets by biological rationale, while also showing where the relevant patients are and how many exist. A target with sound biology and a population too small or scattered to enroll is a problem sponsors should see at the start.

Molecule design follows the same logic. Generative models can propose structures against a target and predict their behavior before anything is synthesized. Insilico Medicine used AI to identify both the target and the molecule for rentosertib, a TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The company reported reaching a preclinical candidate in just under 18 months for about $2.6 million. In June 2025, positive results from a 71-patient Phase IIa trial (NCT05938920) were published in Nature Medicine.

Candidate selection is where I see the most avoidable waste. Teams review animal data, blood panels, and toxicology findings and make a judgment call. When the evidence is ambiguous, programs often advance anyway and stop once human data confirms what earlier results suggested. AI that evaluates preclinical results as a whole, and compares them with outcomes for similar compounds, can flag weak candidates sooner. It can also point to dosing or structural changes that could make a molecule safer.

Regulators are moving this way too. In April 2025, the FDA announced a plan to phase out animal testing requirements for monoclonal antibodies and other drugs, with AI-based computational toxicity models among the proposed alternatives.

Connecting the operations

In my experience, a 60- to 90-page protocol takes a medical writer 90 to 120 hours to compile. A connected system can take a synopsis built on AI-gathered literature and population data, apply the sponsor’s template and produce a draft that is 80% to 95% complete in minutes. That protocol then drives draft case report forms, a statistical analysis plan, table shells and programming.

My team’s current application has the ability to run over 170+ agents, each handling a defined step and passing work to the next. Others report similar gains further along: McKinsey describes a multi-agent system that cut clinical study report timelines from about 12 weeks to six.

Once patient data arrives, the same system can summarize results after the first few patients and flag where key indicators show risk. It can then project how that risk will develop and recommend actions while there is time to take them. Expert corrections feed back in, so each study improves the next.

Small and mid-sized biotechs stand to gain the most. Emerging biopharma companies originated 85% of new active substances launched in 2024, yet many run lean. The head of one small biotech told me he had a strong pipeline and five employees. A connected workflow overseen by an experienced clinical data engineer lets a company that size produce work that once required a large internal staff or a full-service CRO.

How humans keep up

Models alone won’t shorten timelines. Data quality, validation, governance and integration are just as essential. The FDA’s January 2025 draft guidance asks sponsors to establish an AI model’s credibility for each specific use, which depends on audit trails, explainability, and expert review. That makes “human in the loop” review the current industry standard.

Let’s say a particular draft is handled 85% by AI, with 15% review and input from a human. As the technology improves and gets more integrated, that percentage of human involvement might shrink, they might be called upon less and less to apply their own judgement.

And that raises hard questions about where future experts will come from. Today’s reviewers built their judgment over decades of doing this work by hand. Evidence from medicine suggests the risk is real. A 2025 study in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology found that endoscopists’ unassisted adenoma detection rate fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine AI use. Drug developers will need deliberate ways to build expertise, such as simulation-based training, or they will end up asking AI to check its own work.

Connecting AI from target to trial is where the efficiency gains are. Maintaining them depends on something AI can’t supply: a steady supply of people who know what good work looks like.

Rich D’Amato is Head of Data Science, Clinical Development Services, Actalent.
